Your Best Life Now
yor best lyfe now
phrase (slogan)
The title of Joel Osteen's 2004 bestseller and a banner of the prosperity gospel, promising present health, wealth, and triumphant well-being to the believer who thinks positively and claims God's favor. The slogan inverts the New Testament shape of the Christian life, which locates the believer's 'best life' not now but at the resurrection.

Biblical Verdict

🔴
Reject
A prosperity inversion: the believer's best life is the resurrection; now is cross-bearing and often suffering.

Biblical Definition

Scripture locates the believer's best life not in this age but in the age to come, and frames the present as cross-bearing, often through suffering. Paul's settled estimate is the reverse of the slogan: 'For to me to live is Christ, and to die is gain' (Phil. 1:21) — his gain lies through death, in being 'with Christ; which is far better' (Phil. 1:23). The present sufferings are real but light against the glory ahead: 'I reckon that the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the glory which shall be revealed in us' (Rom. 8:18). The Christian's hope is not now but then — 'we ourselves groan within ourselves, waiting for the adoption, to wit, the redemption of our body' (Rom. 8:23). And the way to that glory runs through a cross: 'If any man will come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross daily' (Luke 9:23). 'In the world ye shall have tribulation' (John 16:33). The believer's best life is the resurrection life; now is the time of faith, patience, and bearing the cross after the Lord who bore it first.

Era

The prosperity inversion (Osteen): the believer's best life is the resurrection, not now; the present is cross-bearing and often suffering (Phil. 1:21; Rom. 8:18), with hope laid up in glory.

YOUR BEST LIFE NOW, slogan. The title of Joel Osteen's 2004 book; a banner of the prosperity gospel promising present health, wealth, and triumph.

The inversion: it places the believer's 'best life' in this age, not the age to come.

Scripture's shape: 'to me to live is Christ, and to die is gain' (Phil. 1:21); the best is 'with Christ; which is far better' (Phil. 1:23).

The present age: cross-bearing and tribulation (Luke 9:23; John 16:33), with glory reserved for the resurrection (Rom. 8:18, 23).

Key Scripture

Philippians 1:21 — "For to me to live is Christ, and to die is gain."

Romans 8:18 — "For I reckon that the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the glory which shall be revealed in us."

Luke 9:23 — "And he said to them all, If any man will come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross daily, and follow me."

John 16:33 — "These things I have spoken unto you, that in me ye might have peace. In the world ye shall have tribulation: but be of good cheer; I have overcome the world."

2 Timothy 3:12 — "Yea, and all that will live godly in Christ Jesus shall suffer persecution."

Colossians 3:2 — "Set your affection on things above, not on things on the earth."

Modern Corruption

The prosperity gospel inverts the New Testament: it promises the believer's 'best life' now in health and wealth, where Scripture promises cross-bearing now and the best life at the resurrection.

expand to see more

The corruption is an inversion of the Christian's timeline, and the inversion is total. The prosperity gospel — of which 'your best life now' is the perfect motto — promises that the believer's peak of blessing is available in the present: health, wealth, success, and triumphant well-being, claimed by faith and positive confession. But the New Testament places the believer's best life emphatically then, not now. Paul's death was 'gain' precisely because it ushered him into the 'far better' presence of Christ (Phil. 1:21-23); the present he describes as groaning, 'waiting for the adoption, to wit, the redemption of our body' (Rom. 8:23). The slogan offers as a present possession the very glory Scripture reserves for the resurrection. # voice-lock-ok: progressive: the prosperity-gospel promise of present wealth and triumph is named here to rebut it.

The inversion does its deepest damage to the doctrine of the cross. Christ's call is not to ascend now to one's best life but to take up a cross and follow Him: 'If any man will come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross daily' (Luke 9:23). He promised His people not present triumph but present tribulation — 'in the world ye shall have tribulation' (John 16:33) — and warned that 'all that will live godly in Christ Jesus shall suffer persecution' (2 Tim. 3:12). The prosperity slogan cannot account for the suffering apostle, the martyred saint, the faithful believer dying poor and in pain; on its terms, such a life is a failure of faith. But on Scripture's terms it is the normal Christian life, walking the way of the cross toward a crown laid up in heaven.

The recovery is to set the affections where Scripture sets the hope: 'on things above, not on things on the earth' (Col. 3:2). The Christian's best life is the resurrection life, when the body is redeemed and the glory revealed — a glory so weighty that present sufferings are 'not worthy to be compared' with it (Rom. 8:18). This does not despise present mercies, which God gives liberally; but it refuses to make them the prize. The believer lives now by faith, under the cross, often through loss, with his treasure laid up where 'neither moth nor rust doth corrupt' (Matt. 6:20). Not your best life now — your best life then; and 'be of good cheer,' for the Christ who calls us through tribulation 'hath overcome the world' (John 16:33).

Hebrew Roots

The prosperity inversion (Osteen 2004): the believer's best life is placed now, but Scripture places it at the resurrection (Phil. 1:21; Rom. 8:18); the present is cross-bearing and often suffering.

English: Joel Osteen's 2004 bestseller title, a banner of the prosperity gospel of present health, wealth, and triumph.

Scripture's shape: Phil. 1:21-23 ('to die is gain... far better') and Rom. 8:18 — the glory is reserved for the age to come.

The present age: Luke 9:23 and John 16:33 — a daily cross and tribulation, not present triumph; the best life is then, not now.

Usage

"'Your best life now' promised health and wealth, but Paul's best life was death — 'to die is gain... with Christ, which is far better.'"

"Christ did not call us to ascend now but to take up a cross daily; in the world we shall have tribulation, and glory is laid up for then."

"Set your affection on things above; the believer's best life is the resurrection, not the present the prosperity gospel sells."
